text: Two forty-seven A.M., Eastern. No engineer is awake.
But fourteen AI agents are changing your network.
From Vancouver to Toronto to Montreal, your teams have handed the network to AI agents.
BGP, SD-WAN, firewalls, patching, even incident response.
Twelve hundred changes in one hour. Forty-one reviewed by a human.
So who is watching the agents?
And is your data still in Canada?
IBM SevOne. Sovereign observability, for the age of agentic AI.
Use case one: observe, with Canada first.
SevOne runs in your Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver data centers. Telemetry and agent audit data stay in Canada.
It still sees your U.S. branches, and ties every agent change to its identity, its device, and its effect.
Use case two: anticipate.
At one-twelve, a Devin agent changed an SD-WAN policy. Nothing broke.
But SevOne sees the Toronto to Montreal MPLS link drifting above baseline, and forecasts a breach at eight-forty, before the TSX opens.
With the cause, the users at risk, and the fix.
Use case three: prevent.
A Claude Code agent plans to upgrade both Toronto core routers.
SevOne's pre-flight finds the failover would carry Canadian traffic through Chicago.
That breaks sovereignty. The change is held.
The agent re-plans, and stays in Canada.
Sovereignty becomes a guardrail.
Use case four: react.
A Cursor agent pushes a new WAF rule.
Checkout latency jumps eleven times. SevOne flags it in eight seconds.
It links the anomaly to the change, and the change to the agent, then triggers a rollback through watsonx Orchestrate.
Resolved in forty-seven seconds. The audit trail never leaves Canada.
Use case five: control.
All telemetry, kept in Canada. Every agent change, attributed. And a safe-change score for every agent, based on what it actually did.
Sovereign control. In real time.
Your AI agents act at machine speed.
SevOne observes at machine speed. In Canada.
IBM SevOne. Sovereign by design.
